name: Raspberry Pi 1 Model B
summary: The board that started it all: a $35 Linux computer the size of a credit card, launched in February 2012 with 256 MB of RAM and doubled to 512 MB that October.

video.value: HDMI and RCA composite; DSI display connector

revisions.name: Revision 1.0
revisions.changes: 256 MB of RAM. The I2C pins on P1 are GPIO0 and GPIO1, and pin 13 is GPIO21.

revisions.name: Revision 2.0
revisions.changes: I2C moved to GPIO2 and GPIO3, pin 13 became GPIO27, and mounting holes were added. Still 256 MB at first.

revisions.name: Revision 2.0, 512 MB
revisions.changes: Memory doubled to 512 MB at the same price.

software.note: 32-bit image; the 64-bit image needs a 64-bit model such as the Pi 3 or later.

gotchas.title: Revision 1 and 2 GPIO differ
gotchas.text: Three header pins changed between revisions: pin 3 and 5 are GPIO0/GPIO1 on revision 1 but GPIO2/GPIO3 on revision 2, and pin 13 is GPIO21 on revision 1 but GPIO27 on revision 2. Old tutorials often assume one or the other.

gotchas.title: ARMv6 only
gotchas.text: The BCM2835 is ARMv6. Many Linux distributions only ship ARMv7 or 64-bit Arm builds, so use 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS.

gotchas.title: 3.3 V only
gotchas.text: The GPIO pins are 3.3 V. Do not connect 5 V signals or components to them.

gotchas.title: Little current per pin
gotchas.text: Each GPIO pin can supply up to about 16 mA and all pins together about 50 mA; drive motors and other loads through a transistor or driver board.

mechanical.note: Revision 1 boards have no mounting holes; revision 2 added two.

editorial.history: Raspberry Pi was created by a UK charity to get children programming again. The Model B went on sale on 29 February 2012; demand crashed the distributors' websites, and it shipped with 256 MB of RAM until the 512 MB version replaced it at the same price in October 2012.
editorial.today: Slow by modern standards and limited to 32-bit software, but fine for a headless sensor logger, a retro emulator for 8-bit systems, or learning GPIO basics with Python. Pick a Zero 2 W or Pi 4 for anything that needs a desktop or modern web browser.
